summary: EAP-AKA' lets devices authenticate to mobile networks using the 3GPP Authentication and Key Agreement mechanism inside the Extensible Authentication Protocol. It differs from EAP-AKA by binding derived keys to the access network name and by using SHA-256 based hashing instead of SHA-1. This version covers both 4G and 5G deployments, and updates RFC 4187 and RFC 5448.

plainLanguage.summary: EAP-AKA' is how a phone proves to a mobile network that it is allowed to connect. It runs the 3GPP key agreement inside EAP, the framework that carries many authentication methods. This document is the current specification of that method, and it adds how the method behaves in 5G networks.

questions: difference between eap-aka and eap-aka prime
subtitle: How a phone or device proves its identity to a mobile network over EAP, with the session keys tied to the access network's name.

tldr.problem: 3GPP mobile networks authenticate devices with a shared-secret mechanism called AKA, but the earlier EAP-AKA' specification covered 4G only and did not define the session identifiers and exported parameters that the EAP key management framework requires.
tldr.mechanism: The method carries the name of the access network in an AT_KDF_INPUT attribute, mixes that name into the key derivation so that the session keys are specific to that network, and negotiates the key derivation function with the AT_KDF attribute.
tldr.outcome: This document updates RFC 4187 and RFC 5448 and adds the 5G rules for identifiers and network names, without obsoleting either earlier document.

today: RFC 9048 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4187 and RFC 5448 without obsoleting either, and it was later updated by RFC 9678, which adds a forward secrecy extension to the method.

sections.title: What EAP-AKA' Does
sections.content:
The 3GPP mobile network Authentication and Key Agreement (AKA) mechanism is how a device proves its identity to a mobile network and how both sides derive the session keys that protect the traffic afterwards. RFC 4187 carried AKA inside the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) framework as EAP-AKA, and RFC 5448 defined the improved EAP-AKA'.

This document is the most recent and fully backwards-compatible specification of EAP-AKA'. It updates both RFC 4187 and RFC 5448, and it does not obsolete either of them. The previous version described protocol behaviour for 4G deployments only; this one describes behaviour for both 4G and 5G.

EAP-AKA' is commonly implemented in mobile phones and in network equipment. It is used for authentication when gaining access through wireless LAN networks and, with 5G, directly to mobile networks.

Two things separate EAP-AKA' from EAP-AKA. The first is the key derivation function, which binds the keys derived inside the method to the name of the access network; this limits the effect of a compromised access network node or of compromised keys. The second is the hash function: EAP-AKA' uses SHA-256 and HMAC-SHA-256 where EAP-AKA used SHA-1 and HMAC-SHA-1.

The authors state that the EAP-AKA' base protocol is stable and needs to stay that way. Any extension or variant is to be proposed as a standalone extension or as a different authentication method rather than folded into this document.
sections.plainLanguage: EAP-AKA' is how a phone proves it may use a mobile network, and then both sides derive keys that protect the traffic. This document is the current version of that method. It adds the rules for 5G networks and updates the two earlier specifications without replacing them.

sections.title: The Authentication Exchange
sections.content:
EAP-AKA' follows the EAP-AKA specification in every respect except the changes listed in Section 3. Figure 1 of this document shows the exchange, and each AKA'-Challenge message is the corresponding EAP-AKA message carrying the EAP-AKA' Type code.

The server first sends an EAP-Request/Identity and the peer answers with an EAP-Response/Identity that carries the user's Network Access Identifier. The server then determines the name of the access network and checks that the access network is authorized to use that name. It runs the AKA' algorithms to produce the random value RAND and the token AUTN, and derives the session keys from CK' and IK'. RAND and AUTN travel as the AT_RAND and AT_AUTN attributes, the network name travels in the AT_KDF_INPUT attribute, and the AT_KDF attribute signals which key derivation function is in use. The session keys are used to build the AT_MAC attribute.

The peer works out what the network name should be from its own situation, for example from the access technology it is using, and compares it with the name the server sent in AT_KDF_INPUT. If the two disagree in a way the peer's policy does not allow, the authentication is aborted. Otherwise the peer runs the AKA' algorithms with the received network name, verifies AUTN and the MAC, produces RES, and returns AT_RES and AT_MAC.

The server checks both the RES and the MAC values it received. Authentication succeeds only if both are correct, and the server then sends EAP-Success.
sections.plainLanguage: The server asks the device who it is, then sends a random value and a token. The device checks that the network name the server used matches the one it can see locally, computes the expected answer, and sends it back. The server accepts only if both the answer and its integrity check are right.

sections.title: The Network Name and the Derived Keys
sections.content:
The AT_KDF_INPUT attribute carries the name of the access network for which the authentication is being performed. The attribute holds a type field set to 23, a length field, a two-byte actual length field, and the network name itself. The separate actual length field is needed because the usual EAP-AKA rules express the length in multiples of four bytes; the sender pads the name with one, two or three bytes of all zero bits when necessary. Only the server sends this attribute, and the value it sends MUST be non-empty. If the attribute arrives empty, the peer treats the authentication as failed.

The network name is a UTF-8 string built as the 3GPP specifications define for Access Network Identity. It is structured as fields separated by colons. On the network side the name is a configuration matter, and the authentication server checks that the access network is authorized to use the name before sending it. On the peer side the name is built from local observations, such as the access technology in use or information in a link-layer beacon. If the peer compares the two names, it splits them at the colons, ignores the extra fields of the longer one, and compares the rest character by character, so that a peer that knows only FOO still matches a server that sends FOO:BAR.

Both sides then derive the session keys. For the default key derivation function, with AT_KDF set to 1, the Master Key is computed as MK = PRF'(IK'|CK',"EAP-AKA'"|Identity), where the label EAP-AKA' is an eight-character ASCII string used without trailing NUL characters. The first 1664 bits of the output are split into five keys: K_encr, the encryption key, of 128 bits; K_aut, the authentication key, of 256 bits; K_re, the re-authentication key, of 256 bits; the MSK, the Master Session Key, of 512 bits; and the EMSK, the Extended Master Session Key, of 512 bits. The values CK' and IK' are derived as the 3GPP specification defines, taking CK, IK and the network name from the AT_KDF_INPUT attribute as inputs.

The AKA algorithm must be run with the Authentication Management Field separation bit set to 1, and the peer must check that it is set. On fast re-authentication the keys come from the re-authentication key instead: MK = PRF'(K_re,"EAP-AKA' re-auth"|Identity|counter|NONCE_S), and the first 1024 bits become the 512-bit MSK and the 512-bit EMSK. K_encr and K_aut are not derived again, and it is forbidden to change the network name between the full authentication and the fast re-authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: The server tells the device the name of the network it is connecting to, and both sides mix that name into the keys they derive. A key stolen from one network is therefore useless in another. The device can also check the name against what it sees locally, so a fake network cannot pass itself off as a different one.

sections.title: Choosing the Key Derivation Function
sections.content:
The AT_KDF attribute lets the server name a specific key derivation function. The attribute holds a type field set to 24, a length field whose value MUST be 1, and an enumerated value. The value 1 is the default key derivation function for EAP-AKA', the one that uses CK' and IK'.

Servers MUST send one or more AT_KDF attributes in the EAP-Request/AKA'-Challenge message, ordered by preference, with the most preferred function first. If the peer supports and is willing to use the function in the first attribute, it takes that function into use with no further negotiation. If the peer does not support it or will not use it, the peer does not process the request any further and replies with an EAP-Response/AKA'-Challenge that contains only one attribute, the AT_KDF attribute with the value of the alternative it has selected. If there is no suitable alternative, the peer treats the authentication as failed. The peer also fails if the list of AT_KDF values contains duplicates.

The server checks that the value the peer suggested was one of the alternatives it offered. The first value in the server's own offer is not a valid alternative, because the peer should have accepted it without negotiation. The server then re-sends the EAP-Request/AKA'-Challenge with the selected alternative placed at the front of the list and the whole original list retained behind it, so the selected value appears twice. This is the only situation in which such duplication is allowed.

When the peer receives the new request, it MUST check that the requested change, and only the requested change, occurred in the list. If the peer receives several AKA'-Challenge messages with differing AT_KDF attributes without having asked for a change, it fails the authentication. A request to resynchronize the sequence number is sent after this negotiation has finished, and the AKA'-Synchronization-Failure message carries the AT_KDF attributes exactly as they appeared in the last negotiation message.
sections.plainLanguage: The server lists the key derivation functions it can use, best first, and the device picks one. If the device cannot use the server's first choice, it says so and names another, and the server has to confirm the change in a signed message. A device that sees a change it did not ask for refuses the authentication.

sections.title: Peer Identities and 5G
sections.content:
The identity a device presents falls into four kinds. Regular usernames are external names given to EAP-AKA' peers, and they divide into permanent usernames, for instance ones based on the IMSI, and privacy-friendly temporary usernames such as the 5G Globally Unique Temporary Identifier or a 5G privacy identifier such as the SUCI. Pseudonym usernames and fast re-authentication usernames are the other two kinds. Permanent, privacy-friendly temporary and pseudonym usernames are used with full authentication; fast re-authentication usernames are used with fast re-authentication. Privacy-friendly temporary usernames and fast re-authentication usernames are one-time identifiers and are not reused across EAP exchanges.

The permanent identity is usually based on the IMSI. Exposing the IMSI is undesirable, because a permanent identity is easily trackable and because the IMSI may appear in other contexts as well. Identity privacy in EAP-AKA' rests on temporary or pseudonym usernames, which are similar to but separate from the Temporary Mobile Subscriber Identities used on cellular networks.

Pseudonym usernames and fast re-authentication identities MUST be generated in a cryptographically secure way, so that an attacker cannot tell two identities belonging to the same user from two belonging to different users. They MUST NOT include substrings that relate the username to a particular entity or permanent identity, and no part of a username may be formed by a fixed mapping that stays the same across several pseudonyms for one subscriber.

5G defines the SUbscription Permanent Identifier (SUPI), which is globally unique and used only inside the 5G network, and the SUbscription Concealed Identifier (SUCI), which conceals the SUPI with public key cryptography. The document separates the two uses of an identifier. Where an identifier is used inside EAP-AKA', for example in key derivation, the exact value matters and is fixed by rules. Where an identifier is carried in EAP-AKA' packets, for example in the AT_IDENTITY attribute, the rules say which identifier fills the field.

When the AT_KDF_INPUT parameter begins with the prefix 5G:, the AT_KDF parameter has the value 1 and the authentication is not a fast re-authentication, the peer identity used in the key derivation MUST be as the 3GPP specifications define, and it carries neither the 0 nor the 6 prefix that earlier versions used. In all other cases the identity used in the key derivation MUST be exactly the one sent in the AT_IDENTITY attribute if one was sent, otherwise exactly the one sent in the generic EAP Identity exchange if one was made, and otherwise the identity most recently communicated outside EAP in link-layer messaging.

The method also exports parameters to the layer above. The Session-Id is the EAP-AKA' Type value 0x32 followed by the RAND field and then the AUTN field for a full authentication, or the NONCE_S field and then the MAC field for a fast re-authentication. The Peer-Id is the content of the AT_IDENTITY attribute, or the identity from the EAP Identity Response, or the null string if neither was provided. The Server-Id is the null string.
sections.plainLanguage: A device can present a permanent number, a temporary privacy-friendly one, a pseudonym, or a one-time name for a quick re-check. The document says which of these may be used in each case and which ones may not, and in 5G it also says exactly which identifier text must go into the key calculation so that both sides compute the same keys.

sections.title: Stopping a Downgrade Attack
sections.content:
Negotiating a method inside EAP is insecure: a man-in-the-middle may force the two ends to use a method that is not the strongest one they both support. Since EAP-AKA and EAP-AKA' are expected to be negotiated that way, this document adds a mechanism for EAP-AKA that lets the two ends securely discover each other's capabilities. It is the AT_BIDDING attribute, with a type field set to 136 and a length field whose value MUST be 1. The D bit is set to 1 when the sender supports EAP-AKA', is willing to use it, and prefers it over EAP-AKA.

The server sends the attribute in the EAP-Request/AKA-Challenge message. If the peer supports EAP-AKA', it compares the received value with its own capabilities. If both the server and the peer would have been able to use EAP-AKA' and preferred it, the peer behaves as if the AUTN had been incorrect and fails the authentication, because a bidding down attack may have happened. A peer that does not support EAP-AKA' simply ignores the attribute. Because the attribute appears only in EAP-AKA messages, which are protected by AT_MAC, a man-in-the-middle cannot remove it.

The protection works in one direction only, because the document assumes EAP-AKA' is always stronger than EAP-AKA. No protection is offered against an attack that forces the endpoints to use EAP-AKA'.

The security summary assumes that HMAC-SHA-256 is at least as secure as HMAC-SHA-1. Under that assumption EAP-AKA' is at least as secure as EAP-AKA for mutual authentication, integrity protection, replay protection and resistance to dictionary attacks. Confidentiality and session independence are the same as in EAP-AKA. The key derivation gives an effective key strength against brute-force attacks equal to the smaller of the derived key length and the length of the AKA base key, that is, 128 bits or more, and the transient keys K_encr, K_aut and K_re, the MSK and the EMSK are cryptographically separate. The key derivation negotiation is protected against a bidding down attack from EAP-AKA' to EAP-AKA, because any change is visible in the final AKA'-Challenge message, which is authenticated by AT_MAC, and the peer refuses a change it did not initiate. EAP-AKA' provides no channel bindings, although including the network name in the AKA' algorithms gives a form of cryptographic separation between different network names that resembles channel binding.
sections.plainLanguage: Because EAP lets an attacker in the middle force a weaker method, the server states in a protected message that it would rather use EAP-AKA'. If the device could also have used EAP-AKA', it refuses to continue, since that combination suggests someone interfered with the choice.

sections.title: Privacy, Attacks and Monitoring
sections.content:
Privacy-friendly temporary or hidden identifiers, that is the 5G GUTI or SUCI, pseudonym usernames and fast re-authentication usernames, are strongly RECOMMENDED. The use of permanent identifiers such as the IMSI or the SUPI is strongly NOT RECOMMENDED, because they can be used to track the peer or the user. When authenticating to a 5G network, the SUPI is needed as an input to key derivation on both sides, but that use is internal only, so the SUPI MUST NOT be communicated in EAP-AKA' messages. The SUCI does not give privacy when it is built with the null-scheme encryption, because that makes it equivalent to the SUPI or IMSI; the use of the null scheme is NOT RECOMMENDED where identity privacy matters. The domain part of an identifier, for example the home operator, is typically visible to outside parties even when privacy-friendly identifiers or EAP tunnelling are used.

On attacks, no published attack violates the primary secrecy or authentication properties defined for AKA under the originally assumed trust model, and the same is true of EAP-AKA'. Attacks do exist where a different trust model is in use, where characteristics the design did not provide are relied on, or where participants leak information on purpose. An insider may let an authentication run succeed and then misuse the session keys on the authenticated user's behalf. A serving network may request large numbers of authentication runs for one subscriber, and although resynchronization helps recovery, the sequence number space can eventually be exhausted and the subscriber's card rendered unusable; the attack needs a serving network to take part, and implementations are recommended to track, detect and limit excessive authentication attempts. Resynchronization can also be used to test whether a particular subscriber is in a given area, and with a sequence number scheme that is not time-based the same protocol may leak the authentication frequency of a subscriber.

On pervasive monitoring, the concern for AKA is theft of the long-term shared secret key material stored on the cards, which is conceivable during manufacturing, through coercion of card manufacturers, or while cards and their information are transferred to an operator. The document notes that manufacturing and provisioning processes have gained scrutiny and improved since such reports appeared, and that it is crucial for manufacturers to limit access to secret information and to use secure mechanisms to store and communicate the secrets. Technically, Perfect Forward Secrecy would prevent passive attacks based only on the long-term secrets and observed traffic; it can be added as a backwards-compatible extension to EAP-AKA' or by running EAP-AKA' inside a PFS-capable tunnelled method, and some PFS-capable mechanism is recommended.

Binding the network name into the keys adds protection against key leakage. Keys are specific to one network name, so leaked keys are only useful for providing access under that name: a malicious access point that stole keys from network X cannot claim to be network Y. The server also verifies that the access network's claim matches the name that network should be using, which makes it impossible for an access network to claim over the AAA protocol that it is another access network. If the peer also checks the name it received against what it saw locally, the access network cannot tell one story to the AAA network and another to the peer. These checks prevent some lying NAS attacks, in which a roaming partner claims to be the home network to attract users. The document notes that the benefit depends on how names are assigned: ideally they separate each access technology, each access network and each NAS within a domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Using a permanent identifier on the radio network makes a subscriber easy to follow, so the document pushes temporary and one-time names instead. It also lists the attacks that are known against the underlying mechanism, including a way to wear out a subscriber's sequence numbers, and it recommends perfect forward secrecy so that recorded traffic stays unreadable if the long-term secret is ever stolen.

sections.title: Registry Updates and What Changed
sections.content:
IANA has updated the "Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) Registry" and the "EAP-AKA and EAP-SIM Parameters" registry so that entries pointing to RFC 5448 point to this document instead. The reference for the EAP-AKA' method type 0x32 in the Method Types subregistry now points here, and this allocation can be made with the Specification Required policy of RFC 8126.

EAP-AKA' shares its attribute space and subtypes with EAP-SIM and EAP-AKA, so no new registry is needed. The references for AT_KDF_INPUT, with value 23, and AT_KDF, with value 24, in the subregistry for non-skippable attributes 0 to 127 point here, as does the reference for AT_BIDDING, with value 136, in the subregistry for skippable attributes 128 to 255. A new subregistry for EAP-AKA' AT_KDF key derivation function values records the value 0 as Reserved and the value 1 as EAP-AKA' with CK' and IK'; new values can be created through the Specification Required policy.

Appendix A lists the changes from RFC 5448. The reference that specifies how the Network Name field is constructed now points to the first 5G version of the 3GPP specification, Release 16, which ensures compatibility with 5G deployments. Identifier usage in 5G is now specified. Exported parameters, including session identifiers, are defined as the EAP key management framework required, for full authentication and for fast re-authentication. The requirements for generating pseudonym usernames and fast re-authentication identities are updated to protect identity privacy. The security, privacy and pervasive monitoring material is updated and extended, and a summary of where attributes may appear has been added. The reference updates alone change no protocol function, and Appendix D provides test vectors for four cases so that implementations can check their calculations.
sections.plainLanguage: The document points the official registries at itself and adds one new registry for future key derivation functions. The changes it makes to the earlier version are mostly about 5G: how the network name is built, which identifiers are used, and what the method hands to the layer above.

messages.label: EAP-Response/Identity
messages.note: Carries the user's Network Access Identifier.

messages.label: EAP-Request/AKA'-Challenge
messages.note: AT_RAND, AT_AUTN, AT_KDF, AT_KDF_INPUT and AT_MAC.

messages.label: EAP-Success
messages.note: Sent only if both the RES and the MAC are correct.

viz.caption: THE KEYS DERIVED FROM THE MASTER KEY

items.title: K_encr, 128 bits
items.text: The encryption key, used by the AT_ENCR_DATA attribute.

items.title: K_aut, 256 bits
items.text: The authentication key, used by the AT_MAC attribute.

items.title: K_re, 256 bits
items.text: The re-authentication key, kept for the next fast re-authentication.

items.title: MSK, 512 bits
items.text: The Master Session Key, an output of a successful EAP method run.

items.title: EMSK, 512 bits
items.text: The Extended Master Session Key, the other output of a successful run.

data.title: Key derivation for AT_KDF value 1
data.code:
MK = PRF'(IK'|CK',"EAP-AKA'"|Identity)
K_encr = MK[0..127]
K_aut  = MK[128..383]
K_re   = MK[384..639]
MSK    = MK[640..1151]
EMSK   = MK[1152..1663]

viz.caption: METHOD AND ATTRIBUTE VALUES USED BY EAP-AKA'

items.label: EAP-AKA' method type
items.desc: The EAP method type for EAP-AKA'. EAP-AKA uses 0x17.

items.label: AT_KDF_INPUT
items.desc: Carries the network name of the access network.

items.label: AT_KDF
items.desc: Names the key derivation function; the length field is set to 1.

items.label: AT_BIDDING
items.desc: Signals support for EAP-AKA'; appears only in EAP-AKA messages.

items.label: Default key derivation function
items.desc: The function that uses CK' and IK'.

items.label: Reserved
items.desc: The value 0 in the AT_KDF key derivation function registry is reserved.
